what_it_is: Your hip is a ball and socket joint. The ball at the top of the thigh bone fits into a cup-shaped socket in the pelvis, and both surfaces are covered with smooth cartilage that lets them glide. In osteoarthritis, the wear-related type of hip arthritis, that cartilage gradually breaks down, and the bone, ligaments and surrounding muscles change along with it. Movement becomes stiff and painful, especially after rest.

The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that hip osteoarthritis usually affects people 50 and older, though younger people can develop it. A family history, an earlier hip injury, extra body weight, and a hip socket that formed abnormally from birth (developmental dysplasia) all raise the risk. Symptoms tend to build slowly, and pain often worsens with vigorous activity.
symptoms: Pain in the groin or thigh that may spread to the buttock or knee
Stiffness that is worse in the morning or after sitting
Trouble turning the leg inward or bringing the knee toward the chest
Grinding, locking or sticking in the joint
Pain that flares with vigorous activity
Difficulty with stairs, longer walks, or putting on shoes and socks
Weakness in the hip and leg muscles

how_therapy_helps.intro: Exercise and hands-on care are among the best-supported treatments for hip arthritis. The 2025 hip osteoarthritis clinical practice guideline from the orthopaedic and sports academies of the American Physical Therapy Association gives its strongest grade to manual therapy and to individualized flexibility, strengthening and endurance exercise for mild to moderate hip osteoarthritis. It also supports patient education and functional, gait and balance training. The aim is better motion, strength and day-to-day function.
methods: Joint mobilization and soft tissue techniques to ease stiffness and improve hip rotation and bending, strongly recommended in the 2025 hip osteoarthritis guideline.
Progressive work for the gluteal, thigh and core muscles that support the hip, chosen around the specific weaknesses found on your exam.
Stretching for tight hip muscles plus lower-impact conditioning such as cycling or water exercise, which put less stress on the joint.
Practice with walking mechanics and balance, including proper sizing and use of a cane or walker when it helps you get around more safely.
Learning what aggravates your hip, how to pace activity through the day, and how weight management lowers stress on the joint.

first_visit: Your therapist will ask where you feel the pain, how long morning stiffness lasts, and which daily tasks have become harder. The exam measures hip range of motion in every direction, with special attention to inward rotation and bending, and tests the strength of the hip and thigh muscles. Expect functional tests such as the 30-second chair stand and a timed walk, along with a look at your balance and walking pattern.
recovery: Hip arthritis is a long-term condition, so progress is measured in function: walking farther, sleeping better, handling stairs with less pain. The 2025 APTA hip osteoarthritis guideline describes individualized exercise programs of 1 to 5 sessions per week over about 5 to 16 weeks. Continuing a home program after formal therapy helps you keep what you gain. If pain and function do not improve enough with nonsurgical care, a physician may talk with you about other options, including surgery.
self_care: Keep moving. Regular gentle activity usually suits an arthritic hip better than long stretches of sitting.
Swap high-impact exercise for lower-impact options like swimming or cycling.
Try an ice pack wrapped in a towel for up to 20 minutes, or a warm shower followed by gentle stretching.
If walking is painful or unsteady, a cane or walker can improve mobility; a therapist can size it and show you how to use it.
see_a_doctor: Severe hip pain after a fall or injury
You cannot put weight on the leg or move the hip
The joint looks misshapen or the leg seems shorter than usual
Sudden swelling, or fever, chills or a change in skin color on the affected leg
Pain that keeps getting worse, keeps coming back, or is affecting your sleep

faqs.q: What is the best exercise for hip arthritis?
faqs.a: There is no single best exercise. The APTA hip osteoarthritis guideline recommends individualized flexibility, strengthening and endurance exercise matched to the specific limits found on your exam, such as weak hip abductors or reduced rotation. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons also suggests lower-impact activities like swimming and cycling in place of high-impact exercise. A therapist can help you choose and progress the right mix.

faqs.q: Can physical therapy help me avoid a hip replacement?
faqs.a: It may help some people delay or avoid surgery, but no one can promise that. Nonsurgical care, including exercise, manual therapy, walking aids and weight management, is the recommended starting point for hip osteoarthritis. When pain and function remain limited despite that care, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that surgery may be considered. Your physician and surgeon make that decision with you.

faqs.q: Why does hip arthritis hurt in the groin?
faqs.a: The hip joint sits deep in the front of the pelvis, so pain from the joint itself is often felt in the groin or front of the thigh. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, the pain can also travel to the buttock or the knee. Pain centered on the bony point on the outside of the hip can have other sources, such as the gluteal tendons, which is one reason an evaluation helps.

faqs.q: Should I use heat or ice for hip arthritis?
faqs.a: Either can help, and many people use both. Mayo Clinic suggests an ice pack wrapped in a towel to calm a sore hip, and a warm bath or shower followed by gentle stretching to loosen stiffness. The NHS recommends ice for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours during a flare. Choose whichever eases your pain and lets you keep moving.

faqs.q: Does losing weight help hip arthritis?
faqs.a: Extra body weight is a recognized risk factor for hip osteoarthritis, and the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that losing weight reduces stress on the joint. The APTA hip osteoarthritis guideline also supports education about weight management as part of care. A physical therapist can build a lower-impact exercise plan that supports weight goals without aggravating the hip.

faqs.q: Will a cane help my hip arthritis?
faqs.a: For many people, yes. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says a cane, crutches or walker can improve mobility and independence with hip osteoarthritis, and the APTA guideline recommends teaching proper use of these devices when walking or balance is limited. A cane that is the wrong height or used incorrectly helps less, so it is worth having it checked.

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M16 is the category for osteoarthritis of hip (verified on icd10data.com); billable codes need type and laterality (e.g. M16.11 unilateral primary, right hip).
The 2025 JOSPT guideline also gives a strong grade to dry needling; it was deliberately left out because the clinic does not offer it.
